title: De eximio usu methodi interpolationum in serierum doctrina

deep.reconstruction:
Context (Problem 4, §35). Euler wants a curve y(x), with x = θω, that is odd (y(-x) = -y(x)) and passes through prescribed values at the abscissae n, 1-n, 1+n, 2-n, 2+n, … (in units of θ). These nodes are two interleaved integer lattices, ±n + ℤ, and the curve takes the values p, q, r, s, t, …. He uses the infinite Lagrange interpolation of §25:
  y/ω = 𝔄 p/n − 𝔅 q/(1−n) + ℭ r/(1+n) − …
Here 𝔄 = ∏_{m≠±n} (m²−ω²)/(m²−n²), taken over the nodes m = k±n, k ≥ 1. Since (k∓n)² − n² = k(k∓2n), this gives
  𝔄 = ∏_{k≥1} [(k−n−ω)(k−n+ω)/(k(k−2n))]·[(k+n−ω)(k+n+ω)/(k(k+2n))].
The ratios 𝔅/𝔄, ℭ/𝔅, … follow from swapping one node factor; this gives the formulas at the bottom of p.191, e.g. 𝔅 = ((1−n)/n)·(n²−ω²)/((1−n)²−ω²)·𝔄.

First splitting. Euler writes 𝔄 = 𝔓𝔔, with 𝔓 the product over the k−n factors and 𝔔 the product over the k+n factors. He evaluates each by the §17 rule:
  ∏_{k≥0} (a+k)(b+c+k)/((b+k)(a+c+k)) = ∫x^{b−1}(1−x)^{c−1}dx / ∫x^{a−1}(1−x)^{c−1}dx = Γ(b)Γ(a+c)/(Γ(a)Γ(b+c)).
This gives 𝔓 = 1/[(ω−n)∫x^{−n−ω}(1−x)^{−1−n+ω}dx], which is valid only for ω > n. In modern terms 𝔓 = Γ(1−2n)/(Γ(1−n−ω)Γ(1−n+ω)), and 𝔔 is the same with n → −n.

Second splitting, to avoid the condition ω > n:
- 𝔓' = ∏ (k+n+ω)(k−n−ω)/k² = 1/(Γ(1+n+ω)Γ(1−n−ω)) = sin π(n+ω)/(π(n+ω)).
- 𝔔' = ∏ (k+n−ω)(k−n+ω)/((k−2n)(k+2n)) = Γ(1−2n)Γ(1+2n)/(Γ(1+n−ω)Γ(1−n+ω)).
These are expressed as Beta-integral quotients with (a,b,c) = (1−n−ω, 1, n+ω) and (1+n−ω, 1−2n, n+ω).

Reduction step. Using ∫x^m(1−x)^{k−1}dx = ((m+k+1)/k)∫x^m(1−x)^k dx (correct, it is B(m+1,k) = B(m+1,k+1)(m+k+1)/k), followed by y ↔ 1−y and lowering the x-exponent by one, Euler reaches
  𝔄 = ∫y^{n+ω−1}(1−y)^{−2n}dy / [(n+ω)·∫y^{n+ω−1}(1−y)^{n−ω}dy·∫y^{n+ω−1}(1−y)^{−n−ω}dy].
In Gamma form this equals
  Γ(1−2n)Γ(1+2n)/[Γ(1−n−ω)Γ(1−n+ω)Γ(1+n−ω)Γ(1+n+ω)] = 2n·sin π(n+ω)·sin π(n−ω) / [π(n²−ω²)·sin 2πn].
I verified that this is correct.

Purpose. Substituting 𝔄 gives (next page) an odd interpolation series y ∝ ω Σ ±p_j/(n_j² − ω²) over the nodes n_j. Its prefactor is proportional to (cos 2πn − cos 2πω), which is the 'node polynomial' of the interlaced lattice. Euler then tests it against known cot/csc partial-fraction sums (§39), to see when the interpolant reproduces sin ωθ.
errors: Transcription of the second 𝔓 has denominator ∫x^{n+ω}dx(1−x)^{−1+n+ω}. By the §17 rule (and for the stated value 1/(n+ω)·1/∫…) the exponent must be x^{−n−ω}. The following reduction factor '(1+2n+2ω)/(n+ω)' must then be 1/(n+ω). Either the print or the transcription has a sign slip; the final formula is correct only with −n−ω.
In the final expressions for 𝔄 the second Beta factor must be ∫y^{n+ω−1}(1−y)^{−n−ω}dy, not (1−y)^{n+ω}. The next page uses (1−z)^{−n−ω}, and the Gamma check confirms it.

Gap: the 'alia distributio' removes the restriction ω > n but introduces others for convergence of the integrals: 0 < n+ω < 1 and n < 1/2. Euler does not state these. The identity extends by analytic continuation, which Euler implicitly relies on.

The intermediate line '𝔄 = 𝔓𝔔 = (1−n+ω)∫…' on p.191 is garbled in transcription. The constants (1−n+ω), (1+2n) and (n+ω) are absorbed when the y-exponent is lowered by one, and the end result is consistent.

ideas.what: Infinite Lagrange interpolation for an odd function on the node set ±n+ℤ (two interleaved lattices), with coefficients as infinite products
ideas.modern_name: Lagrange/cardinal-type interpolation series for periodic nonuniform (second-order) sampling; node function cos2πn − cos2πω
ideas.usually_credited_to: Cardinal series: Whittaker 1915, Kotelnikov/Shannon; second-order (bunched) sampling: Kohlenberg 1953; infinite Lagrange interpolation: Euler/Lagrange era generally
ideas.where_published: E555 itself (Opuscula analytica I, 1783); related interpolation in Euler's earlier series papers

ideas.what: Evaluation of infinite products of rational factors as quotients of Beta integrals (§17 rule)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (Wallis-type product theorems, e.g. E122 and later), Gauss 1812 for Gamma form
ideas.where_published: E122 'De productis ex infinitis factoribus ortis' and other Euler papers on Wallis products
Institutiones calculi integralis I; E19 etc.

ideas.what: Closed coefficient 𝔄 for the interlaced-lattice interpolant, equivalent to 2n sinπ(n+ω) sinπ(n−ω)/(π(n²−ω²) sin2πn)
ideas.modern_name: Product formula via reflection Γ(z)Γ(1−z) = π/sin πz
ideas.where_published: Here in integral form; Euler does not convert it to sines on this page

missed.claim: Euler builds an explicit interpolation series on two interleaved shifted lattices ±n+ℤ, with closed-form (Beta/Gamma, hence trigonometric) coefficients. This is structurally the reconstruction formula of second-order / periodic nonuniform sampling (Kohlenberg 1953; Papoulis generalized sampling), whose kernel involves sin π(ω−n)·sin π(ω+n)/sin 2πn. Histories of the sampling theorem (Butzer–Stens etc.) mention Euler's interpolation work, but I am unsure whether this interlaced-node problem in E555 is recognized as a precursor of nonuniform sampling.
missed.quote: Si sit x=nθ, (1−n)θ, (1+n)θ, (2−n)θ, (2+n)θ, … vt fiat y=p, q, r, s, t
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: A priority/history note for sampling theory: an 18th-century derivation of the bunched-sampling interpolant. It includes the degenerate behaviour as sin2πn → 0 (n → 0 or 1/2), which is the known instability of second-order sampling.

deep.surprise_reason: The computations are routine Euler Beta-integral manipulations. The interpolation on an interlaced lattice is mildly interesting as an unremarked precursor of nonuniform sampling formulas, but E555 is known for its interpolation content.
transcription_corrections: Second 𝔓 (p.191): denominator should read ∫x^{−n−ω}dx(1−x)^{−1+n+ω} (sign of the x-exponent), giving 𝔓 = 1/(n+ω)·1/∫x^{−n−ω}dx(1−x)^{−1+n+ω}.
Corresponding reduction: ∫x^{−n−ω}dx(1−x)^{−1+n+ω} = (1/(n+ω))∫y^{−n−ω}dy(1−y)^{n+ω}; the transcribed factor (1+2n+2ω)/(n+ω) is inconsistent.
Final 𝔄 (p.191): second factor of the denominator should be ∫y^{n+ω−1}dy(1−y)^{−n−ω}, consistent with Δ on p.192.
In the intermediate expressions, the exponents after the y ↔ 1−y swap appear as (1−y)^{−2n}, (1−y)^{n−ω}, (1−y)^{−n−ω} with y^{n+ω}; the transcription's (1−y)^{n+ω} is erroneous.
